items.author: liambush20
items.how: (1) The agent schedules its own work and keeps working toward the goals you give it, without waiting to be asked. (2) It holds playbooks, your organization's best practices and knowledge written down, and enriches them as people use it: this is its memory (it is stateful, it keeps state between conversations). (3) Each person connects their own tools (enterprise connectors such as CRM or Drive). It deploys on LangChain's infrastructure (MDA, according to Harrison Chase).
items.title: Persistent Agent: a permanent AI teammate living in your Slack
items.try: Open source, a template to fork over the weekend according to Harrison Chase. Stars and license not checked. The project link could not be opened (t.co), so details are limited.
items.what: An open source blueprint from LangChain for building an always-on agent in Slack. Put simply, the base for an in-house, proactive team assistant that you adapt to your company.
items.who: Teams that want agents doing real work in the company. Most agents are reactive (you ask, they answer); this one pursues a goal over time, like an ops analyst you hand a file to. A good starting point to understand how planning, memory and tools fit together.

items.author: rlancemartin
items.how: Claude wrote a first version in about a week; the real work was proving it behaved the same. (1) Shadowing: each real request goes through the old and the new version and the results are compared step by step. (2) To protect privacy, the text is never read: only a fingerprint of each difference is recorded (which step, which byte, which length). (3) A script groups these differences every 10-30 minutes; a coordinator agent receives each new kind of difference and assigns it to a worker agent, with a Slack thread where engineers follow along and steer. (4) Three loops: an inner loop (sandbox, checks in under a second), an outer loop (validation on production traffic, after human PR review) a…
items.title: How Anthropic migrated its API to Rust with a team of agents
items.try: Public article, worth reading in full to see a real multi-agent system in production.
items.what: The story of rewriting Claude's Messages API from Python to Rust, largely by Claude agents, verified against real traffic.
items.who: The key lesson: with AI, generating code gets easy, verifying it becomes the bottleneck. The code passed 98% of its tests but only about 25% of real requests matched at first. Final result: about 70% less CPU per request and about 20% lower latency.

items.author: samecrowder
items.how: (1) A dedicated database, SmithDB, ingests traces (Clay sends hundreds of millions of events per day). (2) Outcomes are added (the real result: a thumbs down, a merged PR...). (3) Online evals (automatic judges, often an LLM-as-a-judge or a cheaper decision model) label the traces. (4) AI Search lets you search in natural language ("conversations where the user got frustrated"). (5) Agents then analyze these traces to propose fixes.
items.title: Agent Lake: LangChain's data lake for agent traces
items.try: Built into LangSmith (paid offering, free trial).
items.what: LangSmith's new vision: store every agent trace (the detailed log of each step) and run intelligent compute on top to improve agents. Put simply, a Snowflake specialized for what your agents do.
items.who: Once an agent runs in production, thousands of traces pile up without telling you whether it is improving. Useful to understand how a business agent is managed over time.

items.author: karpathy
items.how: All the data is projected onto a grid of 25 km hexagons and translated into game language (gold is GDP, a city's districts are its real industries). 19 lenses, 524 cities, and an Explorer that turns any column for 3,100 counties into a table and scatter plot. 45,000 lines of code in 7 hours.
items.title: Karpathy: a Civilization-style US map built by Claude in 7 hours
items.try: Deployed publicly (link in the tweet), with the source code reachable from the "?" button.
items.what: A vibe-coded side project: Claude (Opus 5.5 in the Claude Code desktop app, ultracode mode) downloaded and combined 31 public data sources (Census, BLS, NOAA, FAA...) to turn them into a game map.
items.who: Proof that an agent can do real data-ops work on its own (collecting, cleaning and reconciling heterogeneous sources). Note: it still skipped a few states, and used half of Karpathy's weekly quota.
